name: PIQA
description: Physical Interaction: Question Answering (PIQA) is a benchmark dataset for physical commonsense reasoning in natural language. The task is multiple choice question answering: given a goal and two possible solutions, a model or human must choose the most appropriate solution, of which exactly one is correct.
creator: Yonatan Bisk; Rowan Zellers; Ronan Le Bras; Jianfeng Gao; Yejin Choi
publisher: Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence
citeAs: Bisk, Y., Zellers, R., Le Bras, R., Gao, J., and Choi, Y. 2020. PIQA: Reasoning about Physical Commonsense in Natural Language.
rai:dataCollection: The dataset was collected as goal-solution pairs using how-to instructions from instructables.com as prompts for annotators. Annotators were asked to glance at an instructable and construct two component tasks, articulate a physical goal, provide a valid solution, and provide a permutation of their own solution that makes it invalid. Annotators were seeded with instructables from six categories: costume, outside, craft, home, food, and workshop. Two examples were drawn per instructable. Additional qualification HITs were run prior to the main annotation stage and validation HITs were run afterwards. Data was collected in batches of several thousand triples and validated by other annotators for correctness. During validation, examples with low agreement were removed from the data.
rai:dataCollectionType: User-generated content data, Manual Human Curator, Document analysis
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The source data was instructables.com, a crowdsourced collection of instructions for tasks such as cooking, car repair, crafting, and manipulating objects using everyday materials.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The dataset was further cleaned using the AFLite algorithm to remove stylistic artifacts and trivial examples. AFLite discards instances whose feature representations are highly indicative of the target label. The train, development, and test folds were automatically produced by AFLite.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Examples with low agreement were removed during validation. The dataset was cleaned of basic artifacts using AFLite. Goals were tokenized by Spacy. For experiments, examples were truncated at 150 tokens, affecting 1% of the data.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators were prompted with links to instructables and asked to construct a physical goal, a valid solution, and a trick solution that sounds reasonable but is wrong, often due to a subtle misunderstanding of preconditions or physics. Qualification HITs contained well constructed and underspecified goal-solution pairs, and annotators had to identify which were well formed with greater than 80% accuracy to participate in the main HIT. Validation was performed by other annotators for correctness, and human evaluation was performed on development data by majority vote.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: During validation, examples with low agreement were removed. This often removed correct examples that required expert-level domain knowledge and were judged outside commonsense. Human performance was calculated by majority vote. A diff button in the annotation interface highlighted where the two solutions differed, improving annotator accuracy and speed substantially.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Annotators were chosen to participate in human evaluation if they achieved at least 90% on the qualification HIT. Annotator pay averaged greater than $15/hr according to self-reporting on turkerview.com and timing calculations.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper argues that PIQA can help advance language representations that capture physical commonsense knowledge useful beyond NLP, including robotic-language applications. It also argues that learning about the world from language alone is limiting and that knowledge should eventually be learned from interaction with the world.
rai:dataBiases: The paper discusses reporting bias as a major issue in physical commonsense because such facts are rarely directly reported in text. Initial unconstrained prompts led annotators toward prototypical solutions and common household tools. To flatten the distribution of referenced objects, annotators were prompted with instructables. The dataset was also cleaned with AFLite to remove stylistic artifacts and trivial examples and reduce annotation artifacts and spurious biases.
rai:dataLimitations: Some examples judged as mistakes were actually correct but required web search to verify. Examples requiring expert-level knowledge were removed during validation because they should not fall under commonsense. The paper emphasizes that models trained on text alone struggle with nuanced physical understanding and non-prototypical situations.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is introduced as a benchmark for evaluating and studying physical commonsense understanding in natural language models. It includes over 16,000 training QA pairs with approximately 2K development and approximately 3K test examples, indicating use for training, development/validation, and testing.
